Looking at the seasonality breakdown for the upcoming week from @AlmanacTrader, editor of the Stock Trader’s Almanac & Almanac Investor Newsletter, the last week of October has historically closed the month on a firm note, and in midterm years Day 21 (Thursday) has been quite strong.

Monday is trading day 18. Over the past 31 years it has been one of the weaker days of the month, with the major indices down about 0.2–0.4%. Tuesday and Thursday have more than made up for it, each adding roughly 0.3–0.5%, while Wednesday has been about flat. Net, the week has gained about 0.5–0.65% for every major index, including the Russell 2000. That has left October up about 1.5–1.9% on average for the large-cap indices and about 0.5% for the Russell 2000.

Midterm years have been stronger again, led by small caps. The Russell 2000 has gained about 1.6%, the Nasdaq about 0.85%, the Russell 1000 about 0.75%, and the Dow and S&P about 0.5%. Some of that gap reflects which years are averaged: the Russell data only start with the 1982 midterm, while the Dow and S&P go back to 1950. The standout is Thursday, the best day of the week for every midterm line, adding about 0.65–0.85%. For the DJIA, S&P and Russell 1000, that one day has matched or exceeded the entire week’s gain. October has finished up about 3–4% in midterm years, compared with 1.5–1.9% for the large caps across all years.

That hands off to November, the start of what the Almanac calls the “Best Six Months” (November–April), and to the midterm election on Tuesday, November 3rd. Historically, midterms have been followed by strength. 

The S&P 500 has been higher one year after all 19 midterm elections since 1950, by about 15% on average according to a Motley Fool count, and by 16.6% according to BNY. Even after 1986, with the October 1987 crash in that window, the S&P finished about 1% higher.

In terms of hyperscaler performance, have we moved past how much capex are they spending to how much free cash flow are they generating?

Despite a robust outlook with Mag-7 earnings expected to climb about 34% this year, above the 29% pace of the S&P 500, according to Bloomberg Intelligence data, and 27% in 2027, a consensus that has moved up aggressively in recent weeks (two months ago, analysts were anticipating an increase of less than 19%), the Bloomberg Magnificent Seven Index is up just 6.5% this year, well below the 11% rise in the S&P 500 Index and the 15% rise in the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index.

“If we get another scenario where we have to lower FCF expectations, that will elevate concerns about the durability of AI spending and the reliance on incremental capital, and that will flow down to the neoclouds and other parts of the market as well,” said Kevin Shea, senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth. “However, if we can get positive revisions to FCF, the market will breathe a sigh of relief that we’ve reached the bottom for negative revisions and that we’re through the most difficult part of the spending cycle.”

🚨 For the first time in history, Chinese automakers have outsold their Japanese rivals in Europe over an entire quarter !

🇨🇳 In September, Chinese brands accounted for 12.7% of European car sales, compared with 11.9% for Japanese automakers, with registrations nearly doubling year-over-year. BYD, Chery, and their competitors are now gaining market share at an extraordinary pace and their success is no longer driven solely by electric vehicles.

📊 In October 2024, the European Union introduced additional tariffs of up to 35.3% on Chinese-made battery-electric vehicles, on top of the standard 10% import duty, but hybrids were not covered. 🇪🇺 China is no longer competing with Western automakers solely on price, it is now challenging them directly in their own strategic segments. With highly integrated supply chains, significant expertise in battery manufacturing and the ability to develop new models at remarkable speed, Chinese brands enjoy substantial competitive advantages. Meanwhile, European manufacturers must finance their technological transition while facing increasing pressure on volumes and margins.

⚠️ Brussels is now trying to restrict Chinese hybrid imports but tariffs cannot restore an industry's competitiveness. BYD is already developing manufacturing operations in Hungary, Chery is preparing production in Spain, and Leapmotor is leveraging Stellantis' European factories. If Europe taxes cars manufactured in China, Chinese automakers can increasingly manufacture those same vehicles directly in Europe.

➡️ Europe can keep raising trade barriers but protecting a market has never been enough to make an industry competitive.

⚛️ URANIUM
Still my strongest conviction of the four.

Last week’s uranium fuel seminar highlighted the challenge: expanding production requires contracts that support financing, reliable demand signals and successful project execution. TradeTech’s latest published long-term indicator stood at $97/lb for September.

My view: broader market weakness can keep uranium equities under pressure, but it does little to resolve the fuel-supply challenge. Utilities need dependable deliveries, and new mines need commercially attractive terms. That remains a compelling setup for patient investors.

🥈 SILVER
Silver edged back above $54 in early trading. Encouraging, but one positive morning doesn’t establish a recovery.

I’m watching whether buyers follow through after the Fed. Softer rate expectations could help; renewed inflation fears could make the bounce difficult to sustain.

🔌 COPPER
Copper starts the week softer after last week’s pressure from the AI-stock selloff and uncertainty over proposed US import tariffs. Supply concerns remain, including potential labour disruptions.

For me, the key question is whether growth fears overwhelm the longer-term infrastructure demand story. This week’s major technology earnings could influence sentiment toward that investment cycle.

🥇 GOLD
Gold recovered to around $4,010 early Monday after losing roughly 4% last week. Lower oil offers breathing room ahead of the Fed.

I want to see whether it can hold that recovery through the policy decision. A sustained easing in rate expectations would make the outlook more constructive.

My approach this week: stay selective, watch the macro reaction closely, and keep conviction tied to fundamentals. Uranium remains where I see the clearest long-term case. ⚛️

I've been doing a lot of my token research with AI agents lately.

I started out giving pretty explicit instructions about what to dig into, but now I can literally say "do a deep dive on [XYZ]" and it'll go off and do some insane research cause it knows what I want

If you want to get your AI thinking along the same lines, here's a bunch of the things I initially asked for:

1. Explain what [XYZ] does and how its best users actually use it, in plain English.

2. Show me fees paid by real users (last 30 and 90 days annualised vs the last 12 months), and how much is just incentives or points farming.

3. Who owns the supply, when are the unlocks, and what have the team and investors sold? Check onchain where you can, because CoinGecko is often out of date.

4. Compare it to its closest competitors on FDV and revenue.

5. Make the bear case as strong as you can, with the best reply to each point.

6. Source and date every number. If you can't find something, say so. Don't guess.

7. Finish with rough bear, base and bull odds and a price for each.

Still absolutely blows my mind how much better Opus 5.5 is compared to anything I used 6 months ago

🗡️ What DeFi Shipped 🚢 (Oct 26)

Solana now finalizes in about 150ms, Balaji's Network School bought Farcaster, and Privacy Pools shipped a big v2:

9 updates worth catching up on:

• @solana switched on Alpenglow on mainnet, its biggest consensus change since launch. Finality drops from 12.8 seconds to about 150ms.

• Balaji's Network School is buying @farcaster_xyz from @neynarxyz, less than 9 months after Neynar bought it. Farcaster becomes the "Network State Protocol."

• @Ledger launched Agent Intent in beta. AI agents can propose trades and moves, but nothing goes through until you approve it on your Ledger.

Interesting idea but think ledger has had a lot of reputational hits lately.

• @0xprivacypools launched v2 on 7 chains. You can send private payments, request money with a link, earn Aave yield, and swap without leaving the pool. Deposits are still screened, so it stays compliant.

• @Pumpfun partnered with @PreStocks. You can trade pre-IPO tokens for OpenAI, Anthropic, Anduril, Neuralink, Kalshi, Polymarket, and more (not open to US users).

• @defillama launched prediction markets that settle on DefiLlama data, built with @Trueo_'s permissionless markets.

• @Kintsu opened a private beta on @CantonNetwork for lending and staking. Testers can supply USDC, borrow against Canton Coin, and stake CC.

• @longdotxyz turned on community basket management for AINX. Holders now vote on what goes in the basket every 7 days and earn fees from AINX trading.

• @papertrade_xyz says PAPER will stay non-transferable for now. If outside perp markets listed PAPER, attackers could short it while trying to drain the bankroll.

The markets are down but DeFi keeps shipping

France has the highest government spending to GDP of the major developed countries.

But total spending to GDP is just one measure of government's impact on the economy, which at increasingly high levels is negative.

It's important to look at all three: government spending to GDP, the deficit to GDP, and total debt to GDP.

Spending tells you the raw size of government outlays. The deficit tells you whether that spending is funded by taxes or borrowed. Total debt tells you the accumulated deficits.

All three follow the same general finding in economics. A little is necessary. A little more is generally good. But there's a point where the benefits level off. Eventually, the improvement in the standard of living flatlines and then turns negative.

Measured on all three together, France is the worst of the developed countries, but the United States is not far behind. The US actually runs a bigger deficit. Of course, one important difference is the reserve currency, but this speaks more to capacity vs negative impact of increasing government size.

Looking at all three also exposes the inflation fallacy. Inflation can reduce debt to GDP, but with most government spending indexed to inflation, the deficit and spending to GDP don't improve, and those carry consequences too.

As the deficit gets bigger, government borrowing crowds out other borrowers. Many point to AI funding getting crowded out, but I think the impact is downstream. If AI is productive and generates returns, it will keep getting funded, and other sectors get crowded out instead.

Housing is the most obvious example. Housing investment has been weak for 4 years, and the recent rise in interest rates will likely make that worse.

France is currently the most extreme case, but many developed nations are in a similar position, with a level of government size and command and control effects on the economy that negatively impact the standard of living.

I cloned part of Notion and Google Sheets to show you what a software factory could look like. Autonomous agents are going to be able to replicate pretty much any software (or anything they can see and interact with).

I built a simple harness to show you what I mean. You give it a URL and then it opens a real browser, clicks around, takes screenshots, inspects the DOM, and captures how the software works.

It turns those observations into a Markdown brief and hands it to a coding agent (I used the Codex SDK, with terminal access and an MCP bridge that lets the agent use the browser itself).

The original app’s JavaScript gets stripped out and the agent writes its own interaction logic. Then it opens the replica and runs the same workflows on both. Types into cells, checks formulas, opens menus. Compares text, values, and screenshots. Measures the pixel differences and keeps fixing what’s wrong until it's done!

What's fun is that you watch the original on the left, the replica on the right, and the agent working underneath. You can click on Compare and superimpose both screenshots. 

Software is going to get very easy to copy so no more excuse to ship crappy software!
